title: Satyavati
hook: Satyavati's husband dies, her proud elder son meets a Gandharva who shares his name, and only one of them walks away
carry: a boy king, a queen mother, a vow

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati in the boat: a mist, a fragrance, and a son who promised to come whenever she thought of him — think of me, and I'll come. What one thing would you ask for? Day seven hundred eighteen.

Two warriors face each other, and they have the same name. One is a prince of the Kurus. The other is a king of the Gandharvas, the heavenly musicians, a powerful one, the text says. The text calls them namesakes, and says the Gandharva came looking for this fight. That's how the story of Satyavati's first son ends. To get there, we go back to the palace, where the fisherman's daughter is now a queen.
screen: `TWO WARRIORS, ONE NAME.` → `THE GANDHARVA COMES TO FIGHT.`

segments.voice: Satyavati has married King Shantanu, on the terms Bhishma's vow made possible. She bears him two sons: Chitrangada, and then Vichitravirya. And before the younger one is grown, Shantanu dies. So now Satyavati is a widow in a palace she came to from a river, with two boys, and a stepson, Bhishma, who has sworn never to take the throne. Bhishma keeps his word. He places Chitrangada on the throne, and he answers to Satyavati as his mother. Chitrangada is strong, and the text says he's proud. He defeats king after king, and comes to think no one is his equal. That's when the Gandharva of the same name arrives. They fight on the field of Kurukshetra, beside the Sarasvati, a long and bitter fight, and the Gandharva, with the tricks of his kind, kills the prince. Notice where the fight happens. Kurukshetra is a name this serial will come back to. Now notice what the text doesn't say. It gives the battle and the funeral rites, which Bhishma performs. It gives no speech from Satyavati. A woman who has lost a husband now loses a son, and the poem is quiet about her. Some readers fill that silence with grief. Some see her steadiness in what comes next, because Bhishma, with her, sets the younger boy, Vichitravirya, on the throne, still a child, and rules the kingdom for him. The house of the Kurus now rests on a boy king, a queen mother, and a stepson bound by a vow. Keep that picture. Everything this week grows out of it.
screen: `TWO SONS, AND A KING'S DEATH.` · `A PROUD SON ON THE THRONE.` · `THE FIGHT AT KURUKSHETRA.` · `A QUEEN, A BOY, AND A VOW.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle into its own pace. Chitrangada believed no one was his equal, the text says, and a challenger came to test it. Bring to mind one thing you've had to win lately that didn't need winning: an argument, a small slight, a point of pride. Don't scold yourself. Just look at it. Breathe in, and notice how much effort the winning took. Breathe out, and let it rest where it is. The bell holds the time.
Satyavati. A widowed queen with one son lost to his namesake, and one boy left on the throne.
Your line: a boy king, a queen mother, a vow. Today, let one small argument go without needing to win it. Day seven hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: When a death comes in a Hindu family, the funeral rites are often led by a son or a close male relative, as Bhishma leads them for Chitrangada in the story.

original.note: Sanskrit Satyavati: the fisherman's daughter who becomes queen mother of the Kurus.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prince who lost a duel.
what it means: a proud prince meets his match, and a boy is left on the throne.
what a scholar hears: the fight is set at Kurukshetra, the field the poem will return to.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (the sons of Satyavati; Shantanu's death; Chitrangada slain by the Gandharva Chitrangada; Vichitravirya installed)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Shantanu dies before Vichitravirya comes of age; Bhishma installs Chitrangada and obeys Satyavati; the Gandharva's challenge over the shared name; the fight at Kurukshetra on the Sarasvati; the Gandharva's use of illusion; Bhishma performs the rites and rules for the boy Vichitravirya.
The length of the fight is given in the text as a number of years; it is left out under the claims rule.
The two readings of Satyavati's silence are unattributed and unranked.
howItsDone generalizes about funeral rites ('often'); a Keeper may prefer different wording.

Editor pass: the Gandharva's 'fight me or change your name' ultimatum is not in Ganguli (which says only that his namesake came for an encounter), so the hook, fork, practice and carry were reworked around Chitrangada's pride; 'buries' changed to 'loses' (Hindu rites are cremation); the open-hand image (used on 712) replaced.
